name: Acamprosate
drug_class: Glutamatergic modulator for alcohol dependence (taurine analogue)
route_note: Oral delayed-release tablets three times daily, started after withdrawal.

discovery.note: Developed as a structural analogue of the amino acids taurine and GABA.

tagline: Glutamate-modulating drug to help maintain abstinence from alcohol
summary: Acamprosate is used to help maintain abstinence in people with alcohol dependence after withdrawal. It is thought to restore the balance between glutamatergic excitation and GABAergic inhibition that is disrupted by chronic drinking. It is renally excreted and not metabolised by the liver.
mechanism: Chronic alcohol use upregulates glutamatergic NMDA signalling; when drinking stops, this leads to a hyperexcitable state that is thought to drive craving and relapse. Acamprosate is believed to dampen this hyperglutamatergic state, possibly by modulating NMDA and metabotropic glutamate (mGluR5) receptors.
Some research suggests that the calcium in the formulation contributes to its effects. The precise mechanism remains unclear.
uses: Maintenance of abstinence from alcohol in patients with alcohol dependence who are abstinent at treatment initiation

history.title: French approval
history.detail: Acamprosate is introduced in France as Aotal.

history.title: European trials
history.detail: Placebo-controlled European trials, including Sass and colleagues in Germany, report improved abstinence rates.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Campral (Forest) is approved in the US in July 2004.

history.title: COMBINE study
history.detail: The US COMBINE trial finds no benefit of acamprosate over placebo, in contrast to European trials.

history.title: Meta-analysis
history.detail: A JAMA systematic review (Jonas and colleagues) finds acamprosate and oral naltrexone both reduce return to drinking.

serious: Accumulation in renal impairment (contraindicated if CrCl ≤30 mL/min)

facts: Because it is not metabolised by the liver, acamprosate can be used in people with alcohol-related liver disease.
